name: SkinPen

card.summary: A clinician-used microneedling pen that makes tiny skin punctures to help smooth acne scars and texture.
card.note: Use in non-clinical settings has been linked to infection reports.

quick.overview:
SkinPen is a handheld microneedling device. It makes many tiny punctures that prompt the skin to repair itself.

People use it for acne scars and rougher skin texture, usually in repeated sessions.
quick.mechanism: Fine sterile needles create controlled micro-injuries; the skin responds by remodeling and producing collagen.
quick.risks: Infection risk rises when done without proper hygiene; officials have warned about spa treatments, especially with blood-based add-ons.

lead: SkinPen is a handheld motorized microneedling pen made by Bellus Medical and used by clinicians for collagen induction therapy, a cosmetic procedure in which tiny sterile needles repeatedly puncture the skin. People use it to soften the look of acne scars and improve skin texture over a series of sessions.[1][3]

The manufacturer's physician-facing page says the controlled micro-injuries trigger the skin's remodeling and new collagen formation, that the device is cleared for improving the appearance of facial acne scars in people aged 22 and older, that a session takes roughly 30 to 60 minutes with little to no downtime, and that three treatments are recommended with results lasting about six months afterwards.[3] These are manufacturer statements; the page gives no study details.[3]

Microneedling in general is also called skin needling or dermarolling, and has been used for scarring and acne; a 2013 pilot study found that combining it with minoxidil treated hair loss better than minoxidil alone.[1] Separately, a 2023 paper uses the name "SkinPen" for an unrelated handheld wound-healing bioprinter tested in rats.[2]

chain: Skin responds with repair and new collagen
angle.text: Controlled micro-injuries prompt the skin to rebuild, which people use to soften acne scars and roughness over a series of sessions.

paras: Collagen induction therapy punctures the skin with many tiny sterile needles. It differs from microneedling used for drug or vaccine delivery.[1] The manufacturer says its clearance covers the full protocol, including a hydrogel used to reduce friction and a disposable sheath intended to prevent cross-contamination.[3]
Microneedling is discussed for scars and skin quality, and in combination with minoxidil for hair. Treatments combined with platelet-rich plasma are described as unproven pending studies.[1]

The manufacturer's page lists contraindications including active skin cancer in the treatment area, open wounds or irritated skin, allergy to stainless steel or anesthetics, bleeding disorders, pregnancy or nursing, and current isotretinoin use.[3] Health officials have warned that PRP-combined microneedling "vampire facials" given in non-medical settings without infection control carry risks of blood-borne infection; in April 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses linked to one New Mexico spa.[1]

No peer-reviewed trial of the SkinPen device was found in the literature searched; the manufacturer reports a clinical study supporting its acne-scar indication but its page gives no details.[3] A 2023 paper uses the name SkinPen for a different device, a wound-healing bioprinter, tested in diabetic rats.[2] A pilot study on androgenetic alopecia reported benefits of microneedling generally.[1]
